analytic.title: End-to-End Schedulability Analysis for Bi-directional Real-Time Multistage Pipeline

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

textClass.keywords: generalized pipeline system, end-to-end schedulability analysis

div.p: In this paper we discuss the end-to-end schedulability analysis for the bi-directional multistage pipeline systems, in which the arriving tasks could traverse the pipeline nodes in either of the two opposite directions. By accounting for the task execution overlap among nodes, we could derive an end-toend delay bound formula for each task, which transforms the schedulability analysis of the task in the pipeline system into the schedulability analysis of that task in a corresponding single node system essentially, then the uniprocessor schedulability analysis theory could be applied to test the schedulability of this task in the original pipeline system. This transformation makes no assumptions on task arrival patterns and thus could be applied to both periodic and aperiodic arrival patterns. We compare this technique with previous pipeline schedulability test techniques and show by simulations that our technique could derive better end-to-end delay bound except when node count is small and the ratio of deadline to period is large.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time applications are becoming increasing complex in terms of system scale and resources involved. Pipeline systems [1], such as server clusters and data processing backend systems, are specific distributed systems, each of which consist of a sequence of certain resources (in this paper the resources are primarily accounted for as processors, also called node). All the arriving tasks execute on all nodes in sequence, i.e. in the same direction, and must exit the system within a pre-specified end-to-end delay bound.

In this paper, we are concerned with more generalized pipeline systems, called bi-directional multistage pipeline systems, in which the arriving tasks could execute in either of the two opposite directions, that is, each task sequentially traverses a path of multiple stages of execution ordered by increasing or decreasing node numbers, as shown by the solid arrows in Figure 1. In [1], the authors presented a schedulability test for uni-directional pipeline systems by reducing the schedulability test of the pipeline system to that of a single stage system. In this paper, we extend this technique to derive the worse-case end-to-end delay bounds of tasks in bi-directional multistage pipeline systems and also make no assumptions on the task arrival patterns. No assumption on the scheduling policy is made other than each task invocation, called a job, has the same priority on all nodes. Furthermore, no assumption is made on whether different invocations of the same task have the same priority. Hence, the delay bounds of tasks could be derived by reducing the bi-directional pipeline system to an equivalent single node system and then using the existing uniprocessor schedulability analysis theory when static priority scheduling policies, such as Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) and Deadline-Monotonic Scheduling (DMS), or dynamic priority scheduling policies, such as Earliest Deadline First (EDF), are applied in the systems. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: we review related work in Section II. Section III describes the system model. Section IV derives end-to-end delay bounds of tasks in the systems, and Section V illustrates how to reduce the schedulability analysis on an equivalent single node system. Section VI extends the system model to a more generalized one. Section VII compares our test with other test techniques. In the end, section VIII concludes this paper and gives our future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Several previous techniques can be applied in the schedulability test of real-time tasks in pipeline systems. In [2], [3], the end-to-end deadlines of tasks are divided into individual stage deadlines and analyze the latency of each stage independently. This technique may lead to pessimistic results since it assumes the worst-case arrival pattern at each stage, that is, all the tasks are released simultaneously at each stage. Holistic schedulability analysis [4] was first presented for fixed priority scheduling in distributed real-time systems, then was extended to offsetbased response time analysis under EDF [5]. This technique uses the worst-case delay of a task on a preceding stage to be the jitter of that task on the subsequent stage rather than dividing the end-to-end deadline into sub-deadlines on stages.

Several statically scheduling algorithm have been presented to precisely test whether a task set is schedulable [6], [7], [8]. Given a set of periodic tasks, such algorithms try to construct a schedule of length equal to the least common multiple of the task periods so that this schedule precisely specify the execution trace of each task. However, these algorithms have exponential or pseudo-polynomial test duration complexity, which is unsuitable for large scale distributed systems with large numbers of stages and tasks.

To avoid the pessimistic worst-case task arrival pattern, the execution overlap among nodes in pipeline systems with preemptive scheduling policies was first accounted for in [1] and the worst-case delay bound of a task consists of two components: (i) a job-additive component which is proportional to the sum of stage execution times, and (ii) a stageadditive component which is proportional to stage count, which transform the pipeline into a single stage system, then the wealth of uniprocessor schedulability analysis techniques can be applied to decide the schedulability of the pipeline. Furthermore, in [9], the worst-case delay bounds of tasks were given in uni-directional pipeline systems with non-preemptive scheduling policies. In [10], tasks are allowed to revisit certain stages multiple times, that is, there may exist cyclic task flows in the pipeline systems. Although the technique presented in [10] could be applied to derive the worst-case end-to-end delay bounds of tasks in the bi-directional pipeline systems, in this paper we directly study the task execution overlap among nodes in the bi-directional pipeline systems and thus could derive better delay bounds, which will be shown in Section VII.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: To derive the worst-case delay of tasks through N nodes of the pipeline system, we consider individual task invocations, which is called jobs in this paper. We now give the notions used in this paper.

Let there be N nodes in the system, uniquely numbered over 1, 2, ...N . Due to the existence of two different execution directions in the system (i.e. from node 1 through node N , or reverse), -→ S denotes the tasks in one direction, and ← -S denotes the tasks in another, as illustrated by the solid paths in Figure 1. Section IV derives end-to-end delay bounds in this case. In sectionVI, we consider a more generalized system in which tasks might skip some nodes, as shown by the dashed paths in Figure 1.

We define function sp(J k ), for each J k , equal to the node set including all nodes except node N , if J k arrives at node 1 first, otherwise sp(J k ) equal to the node set including all nodes except node 1. On each node s, 1 ≤ s ≤ N , each job J k has a node execution time C k,s . Term C k,max1 and C k,max2 denote the the largest and the second largest node execution times of job J k respectively. C k,max1+max2 = C k,max1 + C k,max2 . We denote by A k,s the arrival time of job J k on node s and let F k,s be the time when job J k completes execution on node s. We let D k be the end-to-end deadline of J k , which denotes the maximum allowable delay of J k to complete its execution in the system, that is, J k must exit the system no later than time A k,1 + D k (if node 1 is the first stage of J k , otherwise, A k,N + D k instead). We denote by J 1 an invocation of a task for which the worst-case delay is being derived. Without loss of generality, we assume J 1 ∈ -→ S .

div.p: The bi-directional pipeline delay bound theorem and its corollary derived in Section IV can reduce a given bidirectional pipeline system to an equivalent single node system, then the schedulability analysis techniques derived for uniprocessors can then be applied to decide the schedulability of the original pipeline system. div.head: VI. GENERALIZED SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In Section IV, we considered bi-directional pipeline systems in which each task sequentially traverses all nodes. However, due to certain application requirements, tasks might skip some nodes in its execution direction. To bound the maximum delay of a task T k in such systems, we first view the pipeline system as seen from the perspective of T k and transform the generalized system model to the model defined in Section III as the following steps:
(1) we could define the execution times of each other task T i on all skipped nodes are zero, then the corresponding nodes are added into sp(T i );
(2) the sequential nodes visited by T k compose the nodes in the transformed pipeline system, that is, for any T j , sp (T j ) in the latter is equal to sp(T j ) sp(T k );
(3) reorder the node numbers.

Step (1) and (3) do not affect the schedulability of the original system, but step (2) relaxes each of arrival times of other tasks in the transformed pipeline system so that this relaxation decreases the schedulability of T k by constructing more aggressive worst-case arrival patterns of other tasks. Thus, if T k is schedulable in the transformed system, it is also schedulable in the original pipeline system.

div.head: VII. SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the performance of the schedulability analysis technique presented in this paper by constructing a simulator which models a bi-directional pipeline system. We assume that W i = 1 for any task arriving at the system, in the interest of simplicity. In order to guarantee the entered tasks could finish before their hard deadlines, an admission controller is used. When a task arrives at the system, the controller first tentatively adds it into the corresponding task set in the system, then tests whether the tasks remain schedulable. If not, the controller drops the newly arrived task.

Each arrived task requests execution on a sequence of stages in increasing order of node identifiers by the probability 0.5, and each node in the pipeline system is selected by the probability 0.8. End-to-end deadline of each task T i is chosen as 10 x+1 N i simulation seconds, where x uniformly varies between 0 and DR (DR ≥ 1), which is called deadline ratio parameter, and N i is stage count in the task's route. When the value of DR is close to 0, tasks will have similar deadlines. If the value of DR becomes more greater, the deadlines will differ more widely. Furthermore, the node execution time of each task T i varies in the interval [ 0.9Di

Ni G, 1.1Di Ni G] uniformly, where G is defined as the ratio of total computation time of a task to its deadline, namely task granularity. Each point on each curve in following figures is the average of 50 experiments, each is carried out for more than 80000 task invocations and under system load of N * 100% which is defined as the sum of computation times of all tasks that arrive during the simulation over the duration of the experiment and N is the total node count in the current system. Due to space limitations, we only present results for deadline monotonic scheduling due to its widespread use. Unless otherwise specified, we use the default value DR = 3.

In the rest part of this paper, we refer to our new test process a reduction-schedulability test. We first consider the case of aperiodic tasks. We transform the pipeline system into a single node system and use the uniprocessor aperiodic utilization bound [11] in the reduction-schedulability test to compare with the pipeline bound derived in [14] by varying node count, task granularity and system load while keeping other parameters constant, as shown in Figure 5-(a). The average per-node utilization of the reduction-schedulability test increases with node count and system load, furthermore, the reduced uniprocessor aperiodic utilization bound [11] favors small granular tasks so that the average per-node utilization with G = 1/40 is higher than that with G = 1/20 when node count is fixed. In [14], the authors showed the actual processor utilizations are almost the same when task granularity G is equal to 1/20 and 1/40 respectively, thus, the average per-node utilization of the test in [14] with G = 1/40 is almost the same as that with G = 1/20, both of which decrease with node count and system load, since it does not account for the overlap in the execution of different pipeline node. The technique "metaschedulability test" proposed in [10] achieves lower average per-node utilization than that of our reduction-schedulability test.

In the rest of this section, we concern periodic tasks only and use G = 1/20 as the default value of task granularity. We compare our reduction schedulability test with the metaschedulability test in [10] and the holistic test in [4] when the . We observe that the utilizations for holistic test decrease proportionally with node count in the system. In contrast, our reduction schedulability test and the meta-schedulability test in [10] could sustain nearly the same utilizations when node count increasing and reduction schedulability test outperforms the holistic test except when node count is small. Hence, the results by our reduction schedulability test are not dependent on node count. The meta-schedulability test derives more pessimistic delay bounds than ours, since it views the delay bound from perspectives of the so-called "flow segments", whereas our delay bounds are derived from perspectives of the corresponding jobs and consider the task execution overlap among nodes in the systems. We could also observe that although when the value of DR decreases from 3 to 1, all the achievable per-node utilizations also decrease, the per-node utilizations by our reduction schedulability test just decrease about 5%, comparing with 20% by holistic test. We do not compare with the traditional techniques [2], [3], as they are more pessimistic than holistic test does, which has been shown in [1]. In Figure 5-(c), we fix DR equal to 1, and vary the ratio of the end-to-end deadline and the task period from 0.5 to 7.5 . We observe that when node count increasing, the achievable utilizations by holistic test decrease significantly, while the utilizations by our reduction schedulability test sustain nearly the same utilizations.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper we presented a schedulability test technique for bi-directional real-time multistage pipeline systems. In this test, we accounted for the task execution overlap in the pipeline systems and don't make any implicit periodicity assumptions on tasks but each individual job having its own static priority, which still can be applied to static-priority scheduling and dynamic-priority scheduling policies. Then we could test the schedulability of tasks in a equivalent single node rather than testing the schedulability stage by stage in the original pipeline systems as holistic test does. In the simulation section, we showed our reduction schedulability test always outperforms meta-schedulability technique, and also outperforms holistic test except when node count is small and the ratio of deadline to period is large. In our future work, we will consider the schedulability analysis of such pipeline systems with synchronization relations among tasks.
